passages.title: The Last Bus
passages.text: I knew I was in serious trouble the moment I saw the red lights disappearing round the corner. The last bus home had left without me. I stood at the empty stop, staring at my phone and wondering what to do. Mum had told me to leave the party early, and I had promised her faithfully that I would. Then Sam had started a ridiculous card game, and I had completely lost track of time. Now I had two choices. I could ring Mum and get the lecture of my life, or I could walk the whole way home. The walk would take about forty minutes, along the main road and then through the park. My phone had one bar of battery left. I typed a message to Mum, deleted it, then nervously typed it again. Just as I pressed send, a car pulled up beside me and my heart nearly leapt out of my chest. Then the window slid down and I recognised a familiar face. It was Sam’s older sister, Jade. “Missed the bus?” she asked, grinning. I nodded, because I did not trust myself to speak. “Get in,” she said. “Sam mentioned you’d left in a hurry, and I had a feeling this might happen.” I climbed into the back seat, feeling embarrassed and grateful at exactly the same time. When I got home, Mum was waiting by the door. She simply raised one eyebrow, which was somehow worse than any lecture.

passages.title: The New Kid
passages.text: On Monday morning, a new boy arrived in our class. Mr Patel introduced him just after the bell and explained that his name was Tomas and that his family had moved from a town up north. Tomas did not look particularly happy about it. He sat at the empty desk next to mine and stared at the table. I tried to smile at him, but he never looked up. At break, he stood by the wall on his own while everyone else played football or crowded round the tuck shop. I watched him for a while, because I knew exactly how he felt. I had moved schools in Year Four, and I still remembered that horrible, hollow feeling of not knowing anyone. Eventually, I walked over. “Do you play football?” I asked. He shrugged. “A bit.” “We need one more player,” I said, which was not completely true. He followed me onto the yard anyway. For the first few minutes, he hardly touched the ball. Then someone passed it to him near the halfway line. He flicked it past one defender, then another, and smashed it into the top corner of the goal. Everybody stopped. Even the goalkeeper just stood there open-mouthed. “A bit?” I said, and for the first time that day, Tomas laughed. By lunchtime, half the class wanted him on their team, but he still chose to sit next to me. “Thanks for asking,” he said quietly. I said it was no problem.

passages.title: Lost in the Fog
passages.text: The fog rolled in much faster than any of us expected. One minute we could see the whole valley below us, green and bright in the morning sunshine. The next minute, everything had disappeared behind a wall of grey. I could hardly see Leah, even though she was only a few steps in front of me. “Stop!” called Mr Hughes from somewhere up ahead. “Everyone stay exactly where you are.” We waited anxiously, our boots sinking into the wet grass. I could hear sheep somewhere nearby, but I could not see a single one. It was strange and slightly terrifying, like being trapped inside a cloud. Mr Hughes counted us carefully, one by one. There should have been eight of us, but he only counted seven. “Where’s Ollie?” he asked. Nobody answered, and my stomach turned over. Ollie had stopped to tie his lace a few minutes earlier. I had promised him that we would wait, but then we had kept on walking. Mr Hughes cupped his hands round his mouth and shouted Ollie’s name. Silence. Then, very faintly, came a whistle: three short blasts. Everybody had been given an emergency whistle at the start of the trip, and I had secretly thought it was a bit babyish. Now I was incredibly glad of it. Mr Hughes blew his own whistle in reply. Slowly, a figure appeared out of the grey. It was Ollie, muddy but smiling. “I just followed the noise,” he said, shivering.

passages.title: The Phone on the Bench
passages.text: I found the phone on a bench beside the swings. It was a brand-new model in a sparkly purple case, and it was still switched on. I looked around the park, but there was nobody nearby. I picked it up and turned it over in my hands. For a moment, I thought about how many people would love a phone like this, and then I felt guilty for even thinking it. Somebody was probably panicking about it right now. The screen was locked, so I could not search for a name. A moment later, however, it buzzed, and a message appeared on the screen: “If you have found this phone, please ring this number.” Underneath was a long number. I had no credit on my own phone, so I walked to the café by the gates and explained. The woman behind the counter kindly let me use the shop phone. A girl answered on the very first ring, and she sounded as if she had been crying. “You found it?” she said. “Oh, thank you. Thank you so much.” Twenty minutes later, she came running through the park gates with her dad. She was about my age, and she hugged the phone as if it were a lost puppy. Her dad tried to give me a ten-pound note, but I politely refused. It did not feel right to accept money for doing the right thing. Instead, he bought me a hot chocolate, which felt much better.

passages.title: Grandad’s Shed
passages.text: Grandad’s shed was full of things that nobody else wanted. There were jars of rusty screws, piles of yellowing newspapers and a broken lawnmower that he insisted he would repair one day. Mum called it the junk shop, but Grandad always called it his workshop. One miserable Saturday, he asked me to help him tidy it. We worked steadily for an hour, sorting everything into three boxes: keep, give away and throw out. Somehow, the throw-out box stayed almost completely empty. Then, under a dusty sheet, I discovered a wooden box with a large dial on the front. “What’s this?” I asked. Grandad’s face immediately lit up. “That,” he said proudly, “is the radio I listened to when I was your age.” He described how he used to sit beside it every Saturday evening, waiting for the football results, while his dad shushed everyone so they could hear. “Does it still work?” I asked. “Let’s find out,” he replied, rolling up his sleeves. We cleaned it with a soft cloth, and Grandad checked the wires and replaced a fuse in the plug. Then he switched it on. At first, there was only a loud hiss, and I was certain it was broken. But Grandad turned the dial very slowly, and suddenly a voice crackled out of the speaker. It was a man reading the evening news. Grandad sat down on an old crate and listened, smiling. I simply sat down beside him and listened too.

passages.title: Stage Fright
passages.text: Behind the curtain, my legs would not stop trembling. On the other side, I could hear the hall filling up with chairs scraping, people chatting and a baby crying. In five minutes the school play would begin, and I had the very first line. I had practised it hundreds of times. Now I could not remember a single word of it. My mouth was dry and my hands were horribly sweaty. Mrs Clarke, our drama teacher, must have noticed my expression, because she came over and crouched down beside me. “Nervous?” she asked. I nodded, feeling as if I might be sick. “Good,” she said. I stared at her in surprise, because that was definitely not what I expected. “Being nervous means you care,” she explained. “Every actor feels like this.” She told me to breathe in slowly for four seconds, hold it, and then breathe out for another four. I tried it once, and then again. My heart was still racing, but at least my legs had stopped shaking quite so much. “Now,” she said, “find your mum in the audience and say your line to her. Just to her, and forget about everyone else.” The lights dimmed and the music began. The curtain swept open, and a dazzling spotlight hit me straight in the face. For one terrible second, my mind went completely blank. Then I spotted Mum in the third row, waving enthusiastically. I took a deep breath, and the words came.

passages.title: The Fox
passages.text: The first time I saw the fox, I honestly thought it was a dog. It was late at night, and I had crept downstairs for a glass of water. Through the kitchen window, I noticed something moving swiftly across the garden. It was low to the ground, with a long, bushy tail. It paused beside the shed and looked directly at the house, its eyes glowing in the light from the window. Then, in an instant, it was gone. The following night, I decided to wait up. I sat on the kitchen floor with the light switched off and my chin resting on the window sill. For ages, absolutely nothing happened, and I almost gave up and went to bed. Then, just after midnight, the fox returned. This time, it was not alone. Two smaller foxes tumbled out from behind the shed, fluffy and clumsy, chasing each other round and round the lawn. One of the cubs pounced on the other’s tail. The mother fox simply sat and watched them, completely calm. I hardly dared to breathe, because I did not want to frighten them away. In the morning, I told Dad. I expected him to be annoyed. Instead, he just smiled and said we should leave them in peace. “They were here first,” he said. After that, I watched for them. By the end of the summer, the cubs were nearly as big as their mother. Then, one night, they did not come back.

passages.title: The Power Cut
passages.text: The lights went out halfway through dinner. One second, we were eating spaghetti and arguing about whose turn it was to do the washing-up. The next second, the whole house was plunged into darkness. The fridge stopped humming and the television in the next room fell silent. “Nobody move,” said Dad, which was fairly pointless, because none of us could see anything anyway. My little brother, Kai, started to giggle, and then he started to panic. Mum found her phone and switched on the torch, while Dad went to investigate the fuse box. He came back shaking his head. “It’s the whole street,” he announced. “Have a look outside.” He was right. Every house was dark, and even the streetlights had gone off. Above the rooftops, I could see more stars than I had ever seen before. Mum rummaged in the cupboard under the stairs and found some candles. At first, it felt peculiar to have no television, no internet and no music. Then Dad discovered an old pack of cards, and we played a game called Cheat. Kai was hopeless at it, because he burst out laughing every time he told a lie. Mum was even worse, since she kept forgetting which cards she had already put down. We played for over two hours, and nobody looked at a screen once. When the lights finally flickered back on, we all groaned. Kai asked whether we could switch them off again. Mum agreed, so we did.

passages.title: Looking After Your Bike
passages.text: A bike that is properly looked after is safer, faster and much more enjoyable to ride. Fortunately, you do not need expensive tools to keep a bike in good condition. You simply need to check a few important things regularly. Start with the tyres. Squeeze each one firmly between your finger and thumb. It should feel firm rather than soft, and if it feels squashy, you should pump it up. Riding on soft tyres makes pedalling much harder work, and you are also more likely to get a puncture. While you are there, look for anything stuck in the tyre, such as a sharp stone or a piece of glass. Next, check the brakes, which are the most important part of any bike. Squeeze each brake lever, and make sure it feels firm and stops well before it touches the handlebar. Then push the bike forward and pull each brake in turn. The wheel should stop immediately. After that, examine the chain. A dry, rusty chain will squeak and wear out quickly. Wipe it with an old rag, then add a few drops of bike oil while you turn the pedals backwards. Remember to wipe off any extra oil, or it will collect dirt. Finally, give the whole bike a thorough clean whenever it gets muddy, because mud can hide problems and make parts wear out faster. These checks only take a few minutes each week, and your bike will be much more reliable.

passages.title: Growing a Giant Sunflower
passages.text: Sunflowers are one of the easiest plants to grow, and also one of the most exciting. With a little care, a tiny seed can grow into an enormous plant that is taller than you are. Here is how to give your sunflower the best possible start. First, choose the right position. Sunflowers love sunshine, so pick a place that receives plenty of light for most of the day. They also need shelter from strong winds. Next, plant your seeds in spring, once the weather has started to warm up. Push each seed into the soil, roughly as deep as the top part of your finger. If you are planting several seeds, leave a generous gap between them, so every plant has room to grow. Water them gently and then be patient. After a week or two, small green shoots should appear through the soil. As your sunflower grows, it will need plenty of water. Water the soil around the bottom of the stem, rather than the leaves. When the plant reaches about the height of your knee, push a tall cane into the ground beside it and loosely tie the stem to the cane with soft string. This will stop it snapping as it grows taller. Before it opens, the flower bud turns each day to follow the sun across the sky. By late summer, a huge yellow flower should open at the top, and later on, birds will arrive to feast on the seeds.
